Katie Ashby. Good morning. Good morning. How are you all? Very well. Thank you. Yourself? Good, thank you. And apologies for not getting the messages about how quickly you'd got through everybody else until late. So thanks for- No, no problem at all... letting me back. Look, I will keep this as brief as possible, but thanks very much chair, members of the committee for the opportunity to appear before you today.

My name is Katie Ashby-Coppins. I'm head of legal, and appear on behalf of Voices for Freedom. Voices for Freedom is a grassroots community organization representing more than 100,000 New Zealanders, and our work focuses on human impact of government policy, and promoting informed public participation in matters of national importance.

In respect of the Indian FTA, we have previously made both written and oral submissions on the agreement itself, and appeared before you, and more recently, submissions on the implementing legislation. I don't propose to repeat those submissions in detail here. You have them before you in our written submission. And I just want to focus on an issue that I believe is probably central to the committee.

And if there is some certainty that you can give that you're confident that the issues have been resolved, then we too would get much comfort from that. So, quite simply, Parliament is being asked to legislate despite unresolved uncertainty. And turning to specific provisions of the bill, I want to begin with a broader point about what Parliament's role is, and that is the fundamental constitutional function is to create certainty in the law. Members will often disagree about policy and merits of legislation, and that's totally appropriate

in a democracy. But before the legal effect is given to legal obligations, Parliament should be able to at least say with confidence what those obligations mean. Citizens, businesses, and courts are entitled to know what the law requires of them, and the purpose of the legislation is to create certainty, not to institutionalize uncertainty. Parliament also requires transparency. It cannot meaningfully scrutinize legislation unless it has the information necessary to understand the legal and practical consequences of

what it is approving. Transparency and certainty certainly go hand in hand. Without both, Parliament cannot properly discharge its constitutional role. That is respectively why this committee exists. They exist to identify uncertainty and resolve it before the legislation is enacted, not afterwards. Our submission is not about whether New Zealand should trade with India, nor is it about whether India is an important strategic partner.

We support expanding trade. The issue before this committee is different. It's whether Parliament should implement an international agreement while significant uncertainty remains about what some of its key obligations actually require. When we appeared before this committee during the consideration of the agreement itself, we raised concerns about investment obligations, immigration, labor mobility, financial services, and digital payments.

We expected the scrutiny process to have resolved those concerns, and we're not sure that that has. Instead, the scrutiny process demonstrated that many of them remain unresolved. The reason these provisions matter to this bill is that by passing this legislation, Parliament completes New Zealand's domestic implementation of the agreement and enables it to enter into force.

I would say possibly the clearest examples concern articles 9.2, 9.9 and 9.10. And those provisions work together. The bill does not reproduce those provisions, rather it is legislation that enables New Zealand to bring those obligations into effect. That is why Parliament should be confident it understands their legal operation before it completes the implementation process.

If India believes New Zealand has failed to achieve the investment objective, can India suspend tariff concessions? Despite repeated questioning, no definitive answers have emerged from what I have seen. Instead, the committee ultimately recorded only its understanding of how provisions would operate. Respectfully, Parliament should not have to infer the legal effective provisions before being asked to implement them.

If the committee itself could not obtain a definitive legal interpretation during treaty scrutiny, that is not evidence the issue has been resolved. It is evidence that the implementation is probably premature That is not simply an academic or legal debate. It is one that is a very real debate, and if New Zealand and India genuinely hold different interpretations of these provisions, the consequences will not fall on the negotiators, officials, or members of Parliament.

They'll fall on New Zealanders, New Zealand exporters, and businesses making long-term commercial decisions. Government may say that these provisions are aspirational. India may take a different view. The agreement itself contemplates remedial measures, and the national interest analysis acknowledges that possibility. That uncertainty should be resolved before the legislation is enacted, not afterwards.

That leads to a broader concern. Government appears to have transferred treaty risk onto New Zealand businesses. Businesses are effectively being told, "This is our interpretation. India may have another. You will need to assess your risk yourselves." Respectfully, that reverses where responsibility properly lies.

It is government's responsibility to negotiate agreements whose obligations are clear before they are signed. It is Parliament's responsibility to ensure those obligations are understood before they are implemented. It is not the responsibility of exporters or businesses to discover years later that the parties never shared the same understanding of what was approved.

The second point I just wish to make concerns the economic justification. The government has relied upon modeling projecting modest economic gains. The modeling may ultimately prove correct, and we certainly hope that it does, but let's put into lights that it is modeling, and modeling inherently comes with issues of bias and various other issues.

But Parliament has only been presented with one side of the ledger. Where is the assessment of the opportunity cost of encouraging 20 billion of New Zealand investment into India? Where is the assessment of the consequences if tariff concessions were later suspended? Forecast benefits should never be accepted without equally rigorous assessments of risks.

Finally, this bill is frequently described as technical legislation. With respect, it's only technically drafted. It's not technically insignificant. By passing this bill, Parliament completes New Zealand's domestic implementation of an agreement extending well beyond tariffs, well beyond trade. It reaches into overseas investment, immigration, labor mobility, financial services, digital payments, and future regulatory settings.

It's not about drafting, it's about giving legal effect to international obligations. Chair, I return to where I began. The issue before the committee is not whether New Zealand should trade with India. The issue is whether Parliament should legislate before it has certainty and transparency necessary to discharge its constitutional role. If Parliament itself is still debating what key provisions require, if members have been unable to find definitive answers during the scrutiny process, if the committee's report necessarily relies upon

its own understanding rather than shared legal interpretation, then Parliament has not reached a point where implementation should occur. Passing legislation does not remove uncertainty. It transfers its consequences onto someone else, in this case, New Zealand businesses and exporters. For these reasons, we respectfully ask the committee to recommend the bill not proceed until definitive legal interpretations of at least articles 9.2, 9.9, and 9.10 have been obtained.

New Zealand and India have confirmed they share the same interpretation of those provisions. Independent legal and economic analysis has been undertaken. Parliament has received a full explanation of financial services and digital payment commitments, and the committee is satisfied that the obligations Parliament is implementing are clear, mutually understood by both parties, and demonstrably in New Zealand's long-term national interest for New Zealanders.
